# 3. The state of financial inclusion and credit access

Sections 4 and 5 compare the production technology and technical efficiency of farm households that used credit with those of comparable households that did not. How that comparison should be read depends on what borrowing means in this setting: who has access to financial services and through which institutions, who lends to farm households, on what terms and for what stated purposes, and why most farmers do not borrow at all. This section establishes that context from the same crop farmers used in the estimation. Table 2 reports, for 2012/13 and 2016/17, account ownership and the reasons non-holders give for having no account, the institutions and products through which accounts are held, the distance from the farmer's community to financial and transport infrastructure, and insurance cover; Table 3 follows the loan cycle from application through outcome, source, purpose and collateral to the reasons given for refusal and for not applying. Each entry is an unweighted share of the farm operators in a round or, where the item applies only to a subgroup, of that subgroup (account holders, non-holders, borrowers, rejected applicants, non-applicants); the items and response options are documented in Table S0. Three patterns organize what follows. Access to basic financial services widened appreciably between the rounds, and the widening came through mobile money and savings channels rather than through banks. The use of credit did not widen, and the borrowing that occurred was mostly informal or group-based and, where its purpose can be observed, mostly directed to non-farm ends. And the constraint that non-borrowers report is more often the absence of a perceived need than an institutional barrier.

The first of these patterns is visible in the account-ownership rows of Table 2, and it is a widening from a low base. The share of crop farmers holding an account with a financial institution or contributing to a savings scheme rose from `r tbl_pct("table2", "Has bank account/contributing to a scheme (binary)", 1, 1)` in 2012/13 to `r tbl_pct("table2", "Has bank account/contributing to a scheme (binary)", 2, 1)` in 2016/17, a gain of `r tbl_diff("table2", "Has bank account/contributing to a scheme (binary)", 1, 2)` percentage points (Table 2), consistent with the expansion documented in the national survey reports for the same rounds [@GSS2014; @GSS2019] and with the growth of account ownership across sub-Saharan Africa over the period [@DemirgucKunt2017; @WorldBank2024; @Klapper2025]. Even so, `r fmt_pct(1 - tbl_num("table2", "Has bank account/contributing to a scheme (binary)", 2), 0)` of farmers had no account of any kind at the end of the period, so ownership remained a minority status in this population throughout. Part of the increase reflects the instrument as well as behaviour: the 2016/17 questionnaire recognizes mobile money as an account-holding institution, an item the 2012/13 questionnaire did not carry (Table S0), and mobile money turns out to account for a large share of the accounts held in the later round, as the composition of those accounts, taken up below, shows.

Who remained outside follows a pattern documented across African countries, in which income and schooling are the strongest correlates of being banked [@Zins2016], and the reasons non-holders themselves give point the same way, to income rather than to institutions. Not having enough money or income was cited by `r tbl_pct("table2", "Don't have enough money or income", 1, 1)` of non-holders in 2012/13 and `r tbl_pct("table2", "Don't have enough money or income", 2, 1)` in 2016/17, and an irregular income by a further `r tbl_pct("table2", "Don't have regular income", 1, 1)` and `r tbl_pct("table2", "Don't have regular income", 2, 1)`, so that income-related reasons account for about `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table2", "Don't have enough money or income", 2) + tbl_num("table2", "Don't have regular income", 2), 0)` of non-holders in the later round, in line with the global pattern in which insufficient funds is the most commonly reported barrier to account ownership [@DemirgucKunt2017; @Klapper2025]. Mistrust of financial institutions is the only other reason cited by more than one non-holder in ten, and it rose from `r tbl_pct("table2", "Mistrust", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table2", "Mistrust", 2, 1)`. Distance, by contrast, was cited by `r tbl_pct("table2", "Financial institutions are too far away", 1, 1)` of non-holders in 2012/13 and only `r tbl_pct("table2", "Financial institutions are too far away", 2, 1)` in 2016/17, and cumbersome procedures by little more than one non-holder in a hundred in either round. By farmers' own account, further expansion of physical access would address a small and shrinking part of non-ownership; the binding constraint is the level and regularity of income, which is bound up with the same seasonality and risk of farm income that motivate borrowing in the first place.

If what keeps farmers out of the account market is income rather than institutions, the institutions on offer to those who are in it were nonetheless changing shape. The channels through which farmers hold accounts shifted markedly between the rounds, and the shift was driven by mobile money rather than by banks. Commercial, community and rural banks served `r tbl_pct("table2", "Commercial/community/rural bank", 1, 1)` of account holders in 2012/13 and `r tbl_pct("table2", "Commercial/community/rural bank", 2, 1)` in 2016/17. Because ownership rose over the same period, the share of all farmers with a bank account was almost unchanged, at about `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table2", "Commercial/community/rural bank", 1) * tbl_num("table2", "Has bank account/contributing to a scheme (binary)", 1), 0)` and `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table2", "Commercial/community/rural bank", 2) * tbl_num("table2", "Has bank account/contributing to a scheme (binary)", 2), 0)` respectively; the growth in inclusion came from elsewhere. Mobile money, not elicited in the 2012/13 instrument, was reported by `r tbl_pct("table2", "Mobile money", 2, 1)` of account holders in 2016/17, second only to banks within four years of its appearance in the questionnaire and consistent with the rapid diffusion of phone-based finance documented across the region [@Aker2010; @WorldBank2024]. Susu schemes remained a stable secondary channel, at `r tbl_pct("table2", "Susu scheme", 1, 1)` and `r tbl_pct("table2", "Susu scheme", 2, 1)` of account holders, while savings and loans companies (`r tbl_pct("table2", "Savings and loans scheme", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table2", "Savings and loans scheme", 2, 1)`) and cooperatives or credit unions (`r tbl_pct("table2", "Cooperative/credit union", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table2", "Cooperative/credit union", 2, 1)`) lost ground.

What those accounts are used for changed less than who provides them, and it is a narrow use: accounts store money rather than move it. Savings accounts were held by `r tbl_pct("table2", "Savings", 1, 1)` of account holders in 2012/13 and `r tbl_pct("table2", "Savings", 2, 1)` in 2016/17, current or cheque accounts by about `r tbl_pct("table2", "Current or cheque", 2, 0)`, and investment accounts by fewer than one holder in a hundred. That the mix is dominated by savings fits the place formal institutions occupy in Ghanaian household finance, as somewhere to hold resources rather than to transact, a margin on which household saving has been shown to respond to the inflows a household receives, remittances among them [@Quartey2019]. Among transaction products, cheque-book use rose from `r tbl_pct("table2", "Cheque book", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table2", "Cheque book", 2, 1)` of account holders, but ATM cards (`r tbl_pct("table2", "ATM card", 2, 1)` in 2016/17) and electronic banking (`r tbl_pct("table2", "e-banking", 2, 1)`) had barely registered. The financial inclusion that broadened among crop farmers over this period was therefore a widening of savings and payment access, increasingly through mobile money, rather than a deepening of credit or of transactional banking. Account ownership is accordingly a weak proxy for credit access, which is why the analysis treats credit use, rather than account ownership or the composite financial-inclusion index of Section 2.3 whose construction and loadings are documented in Note S1, as the grouping variable for the frontiers (Section 4), and returns to account ownership and the other service indicators only as dimensions along which the credit contrast may differ (Figure 2 and Table 6). Table 2 also reports how account holders first learned of their institution; that block is not drawn on in the text because the mapping of its response categories is under review, as the note to Table S0 records.

The physical infrastructure behind these accounts improved over the same period, which is the counterpart of the declining share of non-holders who cite distance. The average distance from a farmer's community to the nearest bank fell by `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table2", "Bank", 1) - tbl_num("table2", "Bank", 2), 1)` km, from `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table2", "Bank", 1), 1)` km in 2012/13 to `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table2", "Bank", 2), 1)` km in 2016/17; the distance to a motorable road fell from `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table2", "Road", 1), 1)` km to `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table2", "Road", 2), 1)` km and to public transport from `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table2", "Transportation", 1), 1)` km to `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table2", "Transportation", 2), 1)` km (Table 2). These are community-level measures from the community questionnaire (Table S0), so they describe the environment a farmer faces rather than the farmer's own travel, but the direction is clear: by the later round, whatever kept farm households out of the credit market, it was less and less the cost of reaching a lender.

Against that improvement in reach, the risk-pooling side of financial inclusion did not move at all. Insurance cover is thin and confined to health. Enrolment in health insurance rose from `r tbl_pct("table2", "Health", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table2", "Health", 2, 1)` of farmers and is the only product with any reach; life cover fell from `r tbl_pct("table2", "Life", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table2", "Life", 2, 1)` and pension plans from `r tbl_pct("table2", "Pension", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table2", "Pension", 2, 1)`, and every other product covered roughly one farmer in a hundred or fewer. The survey instrument records no crop or livestock insurance at all (Table S0), so the production risk that borrowing exposes a farm household to is, within the products observed here, uninsured. This is not for want of demand: Ghanaian and comparative evidence finds substantial willingness among farmers to take up index-based agricultural insurance when suitable products are offered [@Ali2020; @OppongMensah2023; @Tsiboe2023]. Uninsured production risk is a recognized reason why farm households under-invest in yield-raising inputs even when liquidity is available [@Dercon2011], and it belongs alongside the liquidity-relaxation story when the credit contrasts are interpreted in Section 5: a household that borrows in this environment adds a fixed repayment obligation to an uninsured income stream.

None of this widening reached the credit market. Credit use did not move with access, and Table 3, which reports the farm operator's own loan record, shows why the two margins have to be kept apart: `r tbl_pct("table3", "Loan applied", 1, 1)` of operators applied for a loan in the twelve months before the 2012/13 interview and `r tbl_pct("table3", "Loan applied", 2, 1)` before the 2016/17 interview. Conditional on applying, `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$approval_glss6, 1)` of applications were granted in the earlier round and `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$approval_glss7, 1)` in the later one, so that operators with an accepted loan made up `r tbl_pct("table3", "Accepted", 1, 1)` and `r tbl_pct("table3", "Accepted", 2, 1)` of all farmers. The share of all farmers whose application was refused fell from `r tbl_pct("table3", "Rejected", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table3", "Rejected", 2, 1)`, but because approval conditional on applying did not rise, the fall in recorded refusals does not indicate more generous lending; part of it reflects the "processing" status that only the 2016/17 instrument offers, which applied to `r fmt_pct(objs$credit$processing_share_glss7, 1)` of that round's applicants (Section 2.2). Extending the definition from the operator to any household member, as the treatment of Section 2 does, raises the credit-use rate to `r fmt_pct(objs$treatment$share_treated, 1)` of the pooled sample, still a small minority. The flat application rate against a rising ownership rate is the first fact to carry forward: whatever the account expansion of this period did, it did not draw more farm households into borrowing.

The borrowing that does occur, moreover, has little to do with the institutions whose reach expanded. Where farmers borrow, they borrow mainly outside the formal banking sector, and increasingly through groups. Group-based microfinance or lending rose from `r tbl_pct("table3", "Group based micro-finance or lending", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table3", "Group based micro-finance or lending", 2, 1)` of loans between the rounds and became the single largest source. Friends and relatives supplied `r tbl_pct("table3", "Friends/relatives", 1, 1)` of loans in 2012/13 and `r tbl_pct("table3", "Friends/relatives", 2, 1)` in 2016/17, informal credit and savings groups a stable `r tbl_pct("table3", "Informal credit/savings groups", 1, 1)` and `r tbl_pct("table3", "Informal credit/savings groups", 2, 1)`, and formal lenders, that is banks and other financial institutions, a declining `r tbl_pct("table3", "Formal lender (bank/financial institution)", 1, 1)` and `r tbl_pct("table3", "Formal lender (bank/financial institution)", 2, 1)`. Relational and group-based sources together supplied about `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table3", "Friends/relatives", 2) + tbl_num("table3", "Group based micro-finance or lending", 2) + tbl_num("table3", "Informal credit/savings groups", 2), 0)` of loans in the later round. This is the pattern that the literature on smallholder finance in the region describes: formal agricultural lending remains a small part of rural credit [@Meyer2015], farmers assemble working capital through informal and semi-formal arrangements [@AppiahTwumasi2019], and savings groups have become an important channel for small loans to poor households [@Karlan2017]. Its terms match its provenance. No guarantee was required for `r tbl_pct("table3", "None", 1, 1)` of loans in 2012/13 and `r tbl_pct("table3", "None", 2, 1)` in 2016/17, cash was the most common security where one was required (`r tbl_pct("table3", "Cash", 1, 1)` and `r tbl_pct("table3", "Cash", 2, 1)`), and land secured only `r tbl_pct("table3", "Land", 1, 1)` and `r tbl_pct("table3", "Land", 2, 1)` of loans, so the asset most often discussed as smallholder collateral secured almost none in practice. Among the few applications that were refused, inability to provide collateral or a trusted guarantor remained the leading reason (`r tbl_pct("table3", "Collateral/trust", 1, 1)` and `r tbl_pct("table3", "Collateral/trust", 2, 1)` of refusals), although these shares rest on few observations. Two consequences follow for identification. A loan intermediated through a group or a personal network is allocated on information the survey does not record, such as standing in the community and repayment history, and its presence in one household is unlikely to be independent of the terms available to its neighbours; Section 4.4 takes up both.

If the source of a loan says who allocated it, its stated purpose says where it went, and that bears directly on the interpretation of the credit indicator; the evidence is available on a comparable basis for 2012/13 only. In that round, when the purpose of a single loan was elicited and the tabulated categories are exhaustive, farming was the single most common stated purpose but accounted for under a third of loans (`r tbl_pct("table3", "Agricultural", 1, 1)`), followed by business (`r tbl_pct("table3", "Business", 1, 1)`), education or training (`r tbl_pct("table3", "Education/Training", 1, 1)`) and ceremonies (`r tbl_pct("table3", "Ceremonies", 1, 1)`), with debt repayment and other uses making up the remainder. The 2016/17 instrument elicits the purpose of up to three loans separately (Table S0), and the harmonized purpose categories printed in Table 3 for that round together cover only about `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table3", "Agricultural", 2) + tbl_num("table3", "Business", 2) + tbl_num("table3", "Other", 2, block = "Purpose for loans (multichoice)") + tbl_num("table3", "Education/Training", 2) + tbl_num("table3", "Ceremonies", 2) + tbl_num("table3", "To pay off debts", 2), 0)` of accepted loans, so the apparent fall in every purpose share between rounds cannot be read as a change in behaviour, and we do not compare purposes across rounds. The 2012/13 distribution suffices for the point that matters here: most household borrowing in this population finances consumption, schooling, social obligations or non-farm enterprise rather than farm inputs, and even loans taken for farming are fungible with these other uses [@Hussain2016]. The credit indicator used in Sections 4 and 5 therefore identifies households that obtained liquidity, not households that invested in the farm, and the survey does not link a loan to the spending it financed.

That leaves the great majority of farmers, who did not borrow at all, and most of them do not describe themselves as rationed. Among farmers who did not apply for a loan, the share giving no need for one as the main reason rose from `r tbl_pct("table3", "No need", 1, 1)` in 2012/13 to `r tbl_pct("table3", "No need", 2, 1)` in 2016/17, while the share citing an institutional constraint, such as interest rates, collateral demands or the unavailability of the amount needed, fell from `r tbl_pct("table3", "Institutional constraint", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table3", "Institutional constraint", 2, 1)`; a financial constraint on the borrower's side was cited by `r tbl_pct("table3", "Financial constraint", 1, 1)` and `r tbl_pct("table3", "Financial constraint", 2, 1)`. The stated institutional barrier thus receded over a period in which the application rate did not move. A stated absence of need should not be equated with an absence of constraint: survey-based classifications of credit rationing recognize that households that expect to be refused, that face high transaction costs, or that are unwilling to bear the repayment risk of an uninsured season report no demand and never apply, so that "no need" pools the genuinely unconstrained with the discouraged and the risk-rationed [@Guirkinger2008; @Kumar2013], and the GLSS does not ask the follow-up questions that would separate them. What the pattern does establish is that the non-user group in the analysis is composed largely of households that, on their own account, chose not to borrow rather than households that were turned away, and that the bottleneck in this market sits at least as much on the demand side as on the supply side, which is the reading of agricultural finance that argues for aligning products with farmers' production calendar and perceived needs rather than for expanding supply alone [@DeJanvry2020; @Meyer2015].

Read as one record, running from account ownership through insurance to the loan cycle, four features of this setting shape the analysis that follows and fix where each is taken up. First, credit users are a small minority, and they differ from non-users in the financing environment they inhabit, with borrowing concentrated in group and relational channels whose availability varies across communities; comparing the two groups against a single frontier would attribute to managerial efficiency what may be a difference in the technology each group operates, which is the case for group frontiers and a common metafrontier (Section 4.2), for making the comparison within a sample constructed to be comparable (Section 4.3), and for the test of whether the two groups share a technology at all, reported among the diagnostics in Section 5.1. Second, the indicator distinguishes households that used credit from households that did not, and the modal non-user reports no need for a loan; the contrast estimated in Section 5 is therefore between borrowers and non-borrowers, not between the credit-constrained and the unconstrained, a limit that Section 4.4 makes explicit and that the loan-application row of Table 6 probes by narrowing the comparison to households in which the operator applied. Third, the loans observed are mostly unsecured, mostly informal or group-based and, where their purpose is recorded, mostly for non-farm uses; whether borrowing of this kind is associated with operating a technology nearer to best practice, with a different responsiveness of output to inputs, or with neither, is an empirical question rather than a presumption, and it is settled on the group-frontier elasticities and returns to scale of Table 4 in Section 5.2 and on the technology-gap and efficiency decomposition of Table 4 in Section 5.3, with the readings the data can and cannot support weighed in Section 5.4. Fourth, account ownership and mobile money spread while credit use and insurance did not, so borrowing households differ in the financial services that surround the loan; Section 5.6 asks whether the credit contrast differs between account holders and others and across the financial-service categories of Table 2 (Figure 2 and Table 6). The frontier estimates themselves are deferred to Section 5; what this section supplies is the record with which those estimates, and any reading of them, have to be consistent.
